big: Two hybrid funds each earn Rohan the same ₹1,00,000 gain, and he sells both after 13 months. One tax bill is ₹13,000. The other is ₹31,200. The name did not decide it. The equity share did.

lines: Will I pay tax like an FD on this hybrid fund?
It depends on one number: how much of the fund sits in equity. Let us see where the lines fall, then watch the tax.

rows.name: Fund A: 65% or more in equity

alt: Three bars of funds with 70, 50 and 20 percent equity, each falling in a different tax bucket
caps: Fund A holds 70% in equity. That is above the 65% line, so it is taxed as an equity fund.
Fund B holds 50%. It sits between 35% and 65%, which has its own rules.
Fund C holds 20%, below 35%. It is generally taxed at slab rate, whatever the holding time.
The test is the actual mix in the fund. The label on the cover does not matter.

alt: Bars of tax paid on a one lakh rupee gain for three funds, sold after 13 months and after 25 months
caps: Rohan is in the 30% slab. The slab rate with 4% cess is 31.2%. Equity long-term is 12.5% plus cess, 13%.
Fund A: ₹13,000 either way. Over 12 months already counts as long-term.
Fund B: ₹31,200 at 13 months, but only ₹13,000 after 24 months, when it turns long-term.
Fund C: ₹31,200 at slab rate whenever he sells. Rates and exemption are assumed. Check with a CA.

h: The tax map, as a table
intro: Rules in short, from the lesson. Confirm current rates with a CA.
rows: Long-term after 12 months, at 12.5% over the exemption
Long-term after 24 months at 12.5%, else slab rate
Generally slab rate, whatever the time
note: The 31,200 and 13,000 figures assume the 30% slab, 4% cess and no exemption used. Your own situation may differ.

q: Rohan's fund holds 70% in equity and 30% in debt. He sells after 14 months with a gain of ₹2,00,000. He is in the 30% slab. Ignoring the annual exemption and counting 4% cess on the tax, what is the tax?
opts: ₹41,600, a short-term equity gain at 20% plus cess
₹26,000, a long-term equity gain at 12.5% plus cess
₹62,400, a gain taxed at his 30% slab rate plus cess
₹13,000, since only half the gain is taxed after a year
why: The 20% rate applies only up to a year. He held it for 14 months, so the gain is long-term.
70% is above the 65% line and 14 months is over a year, so 12.5% plus cess on ₹2 lakh is ₹26,000.
Slab rate applies to funds with less than 65% equity. This one is above the line, so it does not apply.
No rule taxes half the gain. The whole gain is taxed, over the exemption, at the long-term rate.

q: Meena holds a fund with 50% in equity and sells after 18 months, with a gain of ₹1,00,000 at the 30% slab. What is the useful point for her?
opts: It is already long-term, since it was held over 12 months
It is taxed at 20% as a short-term gain, whatever the time
It is exempt from tax, since only funds above 65% equity pay
It is at slab rate now, but turns long-term at 24 months
why: Twelve months applies to funds with 65% or more in equity. This fund is below that line, so 24 months is needed.
The 20% short-term rate belongs to funds at 65% or more. This fund's short-term gain goes at slab rate.
Gains here are taxable. The 65% line decides which rates apply, not whether tax is due.
Between 35% and 65% the long-term line is 24 months. Waiting six more months could cut the tax from ₹31,200 to ₹13,000.

q: A fund called "Balanced Income" holds 20% in equity. A client assumes it gets equity tax treatment after one year. What is the right correction?
opts: The name says balanced, so the middle 24-month rule applies
After one year, any hybrid gets equity rates, whatever it holds
Under 35% in equity, slab rate generally applies at any time
It would be taxed as equity once the client's slab is above 20%
why: A name is no test. The middle rule applies to funds with 35% to 65% in equity, and this one holds only 20%.
The one-year rule needs 65% or more in equity. A hybrid with 20% in equity does not qualify.
Below 35% in equity the fund is generally taxed like a debt fund, and a longer hold does not change that.
Slab does not change the fund's category. The category comes from the fund's holdings.

q: A fund holds 64% in equity and 36% in debt. It is one point under the 65% line. Rohan sells after 13 months. How is the gain taxed?
opts: At the long-term equity rate, as it is nearly 65% and over a year
At slab rate: it is in the 35% to 65% band, under 24 months
At the short-term rate of 20%, since 13 months is short for equity
Not at all, since funds under 65% equity are exempt from tax
why: A fund close to the line gets no equity rate. It must reach 65%, so a one-point gap changes the tax a lot.
The 65% line is a hard cut. At 64% the 24-month rule applies, so at 13 months the gain is at slab rate.
The 20% short-term rate also needs 65% or more in equity. A fund at 64% does not qualify.
No exemption exists for a fund's equity share. The share only decides which tax rules apply.

pts: 65% or more in equity: taxed as an equity fund. Long-term after 12 months.
35% to 65%: long-term after 24 months. Below 35%: generally slab rate.
Check the fund's real mix, not its name. Confirm rates with a CA.
